reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes a paid arbitrage bot with an easy-income promise of approximately $10-$20 per day and directs viewers to purchase access using USDT. It also instructs viewers to connect the bot to a Binance account by supplying an API key and API secret and enabling trading permissions, creating a concrete account-control risk alongside the profit solicitation.

opening.argument: Judge the income language alongside the speaker's qualifications. He says that when prices change, a trade may lose money, which is inconsistent with a promise that every trade succeeds. He also warns against enabling a function for safety, and says subscribers can inspect the code and run it locally. Those statements do not prove the bot is safe or profitable, but they support reading this as a risky trading tool whose limitations are being discussed, rather than a guaranteed-income scheme.

citations.quote: sometimes the price may change and you may lost some profit
Please don't ever enable it with raw function this is for the sake of your safety
You'll have the full code to check for the backup and everything will run locally on your machine .

rebuttal.rebuttal: The quoted daily figure is a promotional earnings claim, but it does not erase the speaker's express acknowledgment that trades can lose money. The API instructions describe connecting a bot to the viewer's account; the speaker also describes local execution. The cited setup therefore does not, by itself, establish that viewers are asked to send their secret to the seller.

citations.quote: sometimes the price may change and you may lost some profit
everything will run locally on your machine .

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A passing admission of losses does not neutralize the repeated daily-income pitch. The description offers automatic execution for a stated daily amount, then gives a USDT payment address, paid tiers and instructions to message a transaction ID. The video also directs viewers to enter an API secret and enable trading. Claims of local execution and inspectable code are the seller's assurances, not independent evidence that the offer is safe.

opening.argument: Much of this presentation teaches an operational sequence: it explains why a three-asset route might return more than the starting amount, shows how trading pairs are considered, and distinguishes a computed opportunity from executing it by hand. The displayed notebook includes profit calculations and an auto-trade section. That context makes the earnings figure part of a demonstration of what the tool purports to do, not proof that the viewer will receive that return. A paid version is mentioned, but the instructional substance remains central.

BUT, it can only drag out the information and you can only do it by yourself, by hand.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening identifies a purchase pitch and API setup, but neither makes the preceding explanation fictitious. The speaker walks through a possible conversion route and a profit-computation function before introducing automation. Nor does a displayed calculation establish a completed trade or a reliably repeatable daily return. The content can be evaluated as a tool tutorial with a commercial ending, even while treating the earnings claim skeptically.

citations.quote: if I convert 100 USDT to ETH and from ETH to BTC, I may have more BTC
The tool allow you to automatically compute the profit the trading after profit for all of the market right?

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The tutorial is the sales demonstration, not a separate purpose that displaces the pitch. The speaker says the bot can earn about $10-$20 per day, then tells viewers to transfer USDT to an address to receive a file. The setup asks them to use an API key and secret for automated trading. A notebook showing calculations cannot substantiate the advertised daily earnings, and the instruction to pay makes the claimed return consequential.

opening.argument: The transaction described is a software purchase: a basic plan computes opportunities, while the higher-priced plan includes automatic trading, with delivery described as a zipped file. The payment request is for access to that product; the speaker describes the bot as running on the buyer's machine. The record does not show the seller asking viewers to deposit trading capital into a seller-controlled account or to send the seller their API secret. A proposed software sale with an aggressive earnings claim warrants scrutiny, but those missing steps matter before treating the offer itself as an account-taking operation.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The cited prices establish a purchase request, not a request to surrender trading capital. The API instructions do create a security question, but the speaker says execution is local and explicitly warns against enabling a function for safety. The prosecution's evidence does not establish that the seller receives the credentials or controls the account; it establishes an advertised paid trading application.

citations.quote: everything will run locally on your machine .
Please don't ever enable it with raw function this is for the sake of your safety
If you want to use the Auto Trade Bot, then the price will be 99.99 USDT.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The absence of a direct request to send credentials to the seller does not resolve the risk of supplying a secret to unverified trading software. More importantly, this is not just a neutral software listing: the description couples the paid auto-trade tier and USDT payment instructions with a specific daily-earnings pitch. The video then instructs viewers to enter their API secret and enable trading. Calling the transfer a product purchase does not remove the income solicitation attached to it.
